body:
Can you write a Godot Engine proposal for this?

I can see that that decompressing Minecraft region files is a valid game use case. I tend to have trouble convincing others of the more niche things in Godot Engine. As far as I know this use-case is covered by Zstd compression algorithm, but maybe you can think of something.

https://peazip.github.io/maximum-compression-benchmark.html doesn't seem to mention lz4. I'm trying to look for evidence this a common compression algorithm even though I know it's used in the ZFS filesystem for an efficient runtime decompressor.

Ok, I just created the [proposal](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/11434).

---

> As far as I know this use-case is covered by Zstd compression algorithm, but maybe you can think of something.

What do you mean by this use case? Do you mean decompressing Minecraft map format?

---

Their [website lists](https://lz4.org/#lz4usedby) quite a lot of big names, including gaming-industry names.

Personally I think it would be better to pack _all_ compression algorithms not used by the engine itself into `GDExtensions`. This type of feature is very encapsulatable, and doesn't need to be shipped with every game. But seeing as though the current API is using an enum, that would probably require some refactors.

> Personally I think it would be better to pack _all_ compression algorithms not used by the engine itself into `GDExtensions`. This type of feature is very encapsulatable, and doesn't need to be shipped with every game. But seeing as though the current API is using an enum, that would probably require some refactors.

It's absolutely possible to implement compression decompression via a dedicated GDExtension without using the builtin enum.

A GDExtension implementing an `LZ4Compression` singleton that provides the required functions would do the trick.

IMO "decompressing minecraft region files" is not a good use case to add another decompression library in core.

> IMO "decompressing minecraft region files" is not a good use case to add another decompression library in core.

It's certainly not the best use-case example, that seems to have been the initial use-case that sparked @Hunam6 to make the PR.

LZ4 is a great compression algorithm with an extremely fast decoder, and it is used all over the place (it's implemented natively in the Linux kernel, if that says anything). If a new compression algorithm was up for vote, those in the know would most certainly throw their votes at LZ4 if I had to put money on it.

> Compression can be carried out in a stream or in blocks. Higher compression ratios can be achieved by investing more effort in finding the best matches. This results in both a smaller output and faster decompression.

In game jams, I've utilized LZ4 to get releases down to teeny sizes. It's great!

This particular implementation is compressing and decompressing lz4 blocks. If you give it an lz4 frame to decompress it'll fail silently and return 0, for example if you give it a file compressed with the lz4 cli.

This is still really useful (probably the minecraft compressed chunk is just a block rather than frames) but should MODE_LZ4 be named MODE_LZ4_BLOCK and a separate MODE_LZ4 should do the work to decompress a full lz4 file with headers and frames? or is this expected behaviour for the godot compression implementations?

> or is this expected behaviour for the godot compression implementations?

This is how Godot works for other compression formats: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/28999

Implementing support for opening the standard file formats should be done separately, but note that ZIPReader can already read ZIP archives.

> (it's implemented natively in the Linux kernel, if that says anything)

No, it doesn't tbh. A lot of things are implemented in the linux kernel which makes little sense to have in Godot (which is a game engine, not an OS kernel, and doesn't have a tiny initrd to load before boot)

> If a new compression algorithm was up for vote, those in the know would most certainly throw their votes at LZ4 if I had to put money on it.

How do you define "those in the know" exactly? And why do you assume that people not agreeing with this choice "don't know"?

> In game jams, I've utilized LZ4 to get releases down to teeny sizes. It's great!

How does this apply to Godot?

How would you `get releases down to teeny sizes` if this is merged that you cannot already do with other compression formats and have better compression ratio (at the cost of a, slightly higher and likely negligible in this context, computational cost)?

Do you have an example in mind?

> No, it doesn't tbh. A lot of things are implemented in the linux kernel which makes little sense to have in Godot (which is a game engine, not an OS kernel, and doesn't have a tiny initrd to load before boot)

I was hinting that if Mr. Torvalds chose to integrate LZ4 into the kernel (_it was used to compress SquashFS_), that might show it isn't a random fly-by-night option that makes this enhancement suggestion seem silly; rather a little weight towards that it could be tangible and qualify for a closer look. I'm aware Godot isn't an OS kernel, and that there are plenty of Linux sprockets and wingdings that don't warrant a place in Godot.

> How do you define "those in the know" exactly? And why do you assume that people not agreeing with this choice "don't know"?

People who have worked extensively with compression libraries and tools, doing audits and research to find the best-of when making tooling and dependency decisions for projects - those types. I make no assumption that people disagreeing _don't know_, but I do assume, with some research those that _actually don't know_ might have a change of opinion after further review. At any rate I wasn't being negative towards anyone who have reasons to not support this enhancement.

> How does this apply to Godot?

Godot is used for developing games and applications. It's nice to compress things for release time, sharing with others, or for local long-term storage. Apart from that, LZ4 has other cool tricks up its sleeves, that may be out of scope for this enhancement support discussion... it does have useful features for real-time application use-cases.

> How would you get releases down to teeny sizes if this is merged that you cannot already do with other compression formats and have better compression ratio (at the cost of a, slightly higher and likely negligible in this context, computational cost)?

LZ4 doesn't have the greatest of compression ratios unless configuration is tweaked, that crown would probably go to Brotli (_I see Godot only supports decompression, however_) or any other number of compression algorithms. Where LZ4 shines is it's speed. I referenced game jams as an example, because speed typically comes into play and getting decent compression at high speeds is always welcome when there is a time crunch. That being said, it is possible to get ratios of 2:1 or better, while still being faster than other algorithms.

Apologies if I upset you and ruffled feathers... My only goal was to voice a positive vote in favor of adding support for LZ4. I've always liked LZ4 along with many, many other algorithms. Can I _personally_ live without LZ4 in Godot? Definitely. Don't include it, and what we have now works just fine. I have a ton of tools and scripts in my toolbelt for compression using a plethora of different algorithms, so _this really doesn't affect me in any way_.

All that being said, it appears LZ4 support is coming to Godot, which is awesome. Godot just got a little bit better!

Right, so it seems to me the use cases reported (minecraft region files, FS-level compression like squashFS) don't really warrant bringing a new third party library in core.

I think if we want to open up to more and more compression options (what about LZMA? That's also in the kernel) we might want to explore changing the compression API so it can be extended via GDExtension without bloating core with more library that less than 1% of the users are going to use (for things that could already be achievable with an extension albeit with less syntax sugar).

Thank you all for your feedback!

Whatever to add LZ4 support is ultimately a matter of opinion. My personal one is that the cost is close to none for almost everyone because the lib is tiny and that for the very few where it matters, I made it so they can compile Godot without LZ4 support thus bringing the cost to the absolute zero.

Something else that came up in this conversion is the ability for GDExtensions to hook in built in functions/enums to add their code.  In the very specific topic of having a duplicate of the built in compression functions/enum is fine (`PackedByteArray.(de)compress()`, `FileAccess.open_compressed()`, `FileAccess.CompressionMode`) although not ideal. Otherwise, in other topics, being able to hook into built in functions would be very desirable (think of [mixins for Minecraft type of hooking](https://github.com/SpongePowered/Mixin)).
I don't think I ever mentioned this but for people reading this, you might be interested in the [More Compression](https://godotengine.org/asset-library/asset/3608) addon I developed early January.
Seeing as the concensus internally hasn't shifted, I'll be closing this PR to not give any false impressions. Thanks for your contribution!
